newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sega's interim profits rise on firm sales.
newsitem.headline: Sega's interim profits rise on firm sales.

text.p: Japanese game machine maker Sega Enterprises Ltd said on Friday that its half-year profit grew nearly 16 percent thanks to robust sales.

The company announced sales of 174.9 billion yen ($1.57 billion) in sales in the six months to September 30, up 11.8 percent from a year earlier. It said its parent current profit rose 15.6 percent to 12.8 billion yen ($115 million).
The half-year earnings were buoyed by firm sales of commercial-use amusement equipment, including quick photo machines and on-line Karaoke sets, the company said in a statement.
Quick photo machines have become a hit in Japanese game centres and are especially popular among teenage girls. On-line karaoke systems allow users to download songs via a telephone line.
Sega said domestic sales of its 32-bit home game machine, Sega Saturn, were also firm.

However, the exports were sluggish due to intensified competition in the 32-bit video game machine sector, the statement said. Sony Computer Entertainment Inc, a unit of Sony Corp, also markets a 32-bit game console, PlayStation, in the United States and Europe.
The shift from 16-bit machines to 32-bit machines in the overseas markets also reduced sales, Sega said.
However the yen's retreat against the dollar helped to increase yen-denominated income from overseas sales, a spokesman said.
Sega also opened two large-scale amusement parks in Japan in the first half which gave an additional boost to the sales.
For the full year to March 31, the company expects sales to total 380 billion yen ($3.42 billion) and parent current profit to reach 33 billion yen ($297 million).
Current profit is pre-tax and includes gains and losses on securities investments and other non-operating activities.
"We are counting on firm sales during this year's Christmas season in overseas markets, especially the U.S.," the spokesman said.
Sega is also entering a new business area. On November 24 it will start selling low-priced digital cameras in Japan in a bid to tap a booming market.
Its camera, priced at 29,800 yen ($268), will be the cheapest digital camera in Japan. ($1=111 yen)
